title: NHC earliest reasonable arrival times of tropical-storm-force winds (2018-2025, 294 storms) came after the observed onset in 14-29% of cases, not 10%; the excess was in large Atlantic storms
abstract: Question: are the National Hurricane Center (NHC) arrival and departure times of sustained 34-kt winds calibrated, and which forecast parts cause errors? Approach: we wrote a plan before matching, then compared 6,086 archived Atlantic and eastern and central Pacific base-data files of 2018-2025 with onsets and departures in the final HURDAT2 best tracks (1.14 million advisory-point cases, 294 storms). A best-track radius is a maximum extent, so we used two area rules (P: 0.86 times the radius, the product rule; Q: the full radius) and two time comparisons (10-min, and whole hours in the product's favour). Results: observed onsets came before the earliest reasonable time (stated 10%) in 0.208 (95% storm-bootstrap 0.167-0.251) of cases for rule P and 0.287 (0.240-0.331) for rule Q; with whole-hour times 0.144 (0.106-0.185) and 0.224 (0.178-0.266). The excess was in large storms (mean 34-kt radius above 70 n mi: 0.17-0.35) and Atlantic storms (0.17-0.32). Small storms (0.06-0.13) and eastern Pacific storms (0.04-0.14) were near calibrated or conservative. At leads of 12 h or less the share was 0.14-0.54. Until 2025 the model had almost no hour-0 spread, and a larger final best-track radius at the advisory time raised the 0-12 h share to 0.49 (rule P). Against the official deterministic forecast, onsets were 1.24 h early on average: 0.73 h from 34-kt radius errors and 0.51 h from track errors (Atlantic 0.93 and 0.59 h; eastern Pacific near zero). Late departures were found only with pooled weights. In 2026 the base data gained hour-0 spread, but an exploratory check did not show a smaller short-lead excess under rule Q. A 1-3 h earlier shift fitted on 2018-2023 gave 2024-2025 shares of 0.09-0.17 (exploratory). Limitations: the truth is a best-track wind area, not station data; the size of the excess depends on the area rule and time rounding; neighbouring cases are dependent.

display.caption: Observed shares of the four pre-registered timing statistics (2018-2025, 294 storms) against stated levels. Blue: rule P (0.86 x radius); orange: rule Q (quadrant maximum). Filled: 10-min observed times; hollow: whole-hour comparison in the product's favour; square: equal storm weight. Error bars: 95% storm-cluster bootstrap.

citations.reason: We reuse its HURDAT2 and ATCF parsing and download code and its 0.86 product radius factor. Our timing results show the same storm-size error and the same 2026 hour-0 change in a second NHC product.
Its wind speed probabilities were too low in the Atlantic and too high in the eastern Pacific; our arrival times show the same basin pattern.
